name: The Replication Crisis
description: Large-scale, coordinated attempts to directly replicate published psychology findings have repeatedly found that only roughly a third to two-thirds of original results reproduce with a statistically significant effect in the same direction, and that replicated effect sizes typically shrink to about half the originally published magnitude -- a systemic, field-wide pattern documented across multiple independent large-scale projects, not an isolated embarrassment confined to a few disproven studies.
design_relevance_note: The single most important calibration fact for anyone citing 'science says' in a design rationale: even a published, peer-reviewed, well-cited finding has a real, quantifiable chance of not holding up under direct replication -- a reason to check this corpus's own replication_status field on any cited Finding rather than treating publication itself as sufficient evidence.
prevalence_note: Foundational to how confidently any behavioral-science claim should be cited in design practice -- underlies this corpus's own entire dialectic-verification methodology and replication_status schema field, even though the term itself is more discussed in academic/science-journalism circles than everyday product-design vocabulary.

findings.description: A large-scale coordinated replication of 100 psychology experiments from top journals found only about 36% of replications produced statistically significant results matching the original (vs. 97% of the original studies), with replication effect sizes averaging roughly half the magnitude of the original studies.
findings.effect_size: 36% of replications significant (vs. 97% originals); ~50% average effect-size retention
findings.source_title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science

findings.description: Across preregistered direct replications of 28 classic and contemporary psychology effects run in 125 samples spanning 36 countries (N = 15,305), replication effect sizes were systematically smaller than the originally published effect sizes (median Cohen's d fell from 0.60 in the originals to 0.15 in the replications), and only about half the effects reached conventional statistical significance in the same direction as the original. Despite this general replication shortfall, exploratory comparisons found little heterogeneity in effect sizes specifically between WEIRD and less-WEIRD cultural samples — cumulatively, variability in results was attributable far more to which effect was being studied than to the culture, sample, or setting it was studied in.
findings.effect_size: 54% of 28 replications significant, same direction as original (50% at strict p<.0001); median Cohen's d fell from 0.60 (original) to 0.15 (replication); little heterogeneity attributable to WEIRD vs. less-WEIRD sample split specifically
findings.source_title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
findings.source_venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

findings.description: An independent large-scale replication project (21 experimental social-science studies from Nature and Science, 2010–2015) found only 62% replicated with a statistically significant effect in the same direction, and replication effect sizes averaged about 50% of the original — corroborating a broad, cross-disciplinary replication-rate problem rather than one specific to a single journal or subfield.
findings.effect_size: 62% replicated significant, same direction; ~50% average effect-size retention
findings.source_title: Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015

applications.title: The Federal Reserve's own economists: 'economics research is usually not replicable'
applications.description: Federal Reserve Board economists Andrew C. Chang and Phillip Li attempted to replicate the key qualitative result of 67 empirical papers published in 13 well-regarded economics journals using the authors' own provided data and code. Without contacting the original authors, they successfully replicated only 22 of 67 papers (33%); even with the original authors' direct assistance, replication succeeded for just 29 of 59 eligible papers (49%) -- leading the authors to conclude in an official Federal Reserve working paper that 'economics research is usually not replicable.' A concrete demonstration that the replication crisis documented in psychology extends to a field with very different methods, incentives, and data (mostly non-experimental, often confidential or proprietary), and that the finding comes from within the discipline's own central bank, not an outside critic.
applications.industry_context: academic economics research / central banking research division
applications.ethical_note: A self-critical finding published by a national central bank's own research staff about their own discipline -- illustrates the replication crisis being taken seriously as a methodological problem to fix (the paper closes with recommendations for improving replicability) rather than a hostile takedown from outside the field.
